title_r: Temporal Framing for Pro-Environmental Attitudes: Replications and Extensions of Baldwin & Lammers (2016)
abstract_r: More conservative people are more likely to reject climate protection policies than more liberal people (Bateman & O'Connor, 2016). As Climate protection gets more and more important, it is crucial to find a way to communicate climate change issues and solutions to appeal for conservatives (Baldwin & Lammers, 2016). In their study, Baldwin & Lammers (2016) theorized that the groups might prefer different temporal comparisons for many different reasons, for example because conservatives tend to compare the present with the past and liberals tend to compare the present with the future. Since appeals for climate protection measures are often formulated in terms of the future, they are probably not convincing for conservatives (Baldwin & Lammers, 2016). The idea is to provide the appeals with a past-related comparison (ibid.). In the studies by Baldwin & Lammers (2016), past-related comparisons led to stronger pro-environmental attitudes and more pro-environmental behavior among more conservative individuals. However, the current study situation is mixed: in some cases the effect could not be replicated (Kim et al., 2021; Stanley et al., 2021), in others it could (Herberz et al., 2023). The aim of the planned study is to investigate this effect again by also extending their work and adding a present frame to the past and the future frame. It will investigate whether conservatives show stronger pro-environmental approval of a text and stronger support for an environmental protection measure when it is formulated in terms of the past or present compared to a future-oriented formulation. This is also the outcome we expect. In addition, it will be investigated whether this effect is mediated by the psychological perception of distance and whether a past- or present-oriented frame reduces the perceived temporal and hypothetical distance of climate change among conservatives compared to a future-oriented frame. Here we assume that psychological distance only has an effect on conservatives, since liberals' pro-evironmental attitudes tend to be less influenced by framing.

title_r: Replication and extension of: Large language models associate Muslims with violence by Abid et al., 2021
abstract_r: The main purpose of this study is to replicate and extend the results in Abid et al. (2021; Nature Machine Intelligence). Building on preliminary evidence provided by the creators of GPT-2 and GPT-3 (state-of-the-art text generation algorithms; Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020), the authors showed biased automated text generation when religious identities are cued in text completion prompts. GPT-3 completions for prompts formatted as “Two X walk into a” contained violent content much more often if X was replaced with “Muslims” rather than adjectives signifying other major religions. Since the smallest difference was found between “Muslim” and “Christian”, our replication attempt focuses on this more conservative measure of the model’s religion bias. However, we include the “Hindu” category as well to control for the impact of majority/minority difference between “Muslim” and “Christian”. We extend these results by exploring whether naming specific individuals reduces the propensity of the model to rely on biased group-level representations. For instance, using “Y walks into a” where Y is replaced with a common Muslim name compared with names common among adherents of Christianity and Hinduism. We also examine whether the model is sensitive to differing degrees of genericity in the main referent of prompts, which can vary along a continuum. Generic kinds like “Muslim” lie near one end of the spectrum. Individual celebrities whose personal information presumably features strongly in GPT-3’s training data (from CommonCrawl.org), lie near the other end. Common names associated with social kinds like “Muslim” (e.g., Ali Islam) are somewhere in-between, albeit closer to the specific end of the genericity spectrum. We expect reduced bias as the specificity of the prompts are increased.

title_r: Experiment 1 - Replicating and extending Summers et al. (2021)
abstract_r: This study is part of a research project aiming to explore pain perception biases in different contexts (including physical, psychological and social pain), in turn seeking to better understand and address the factors that contribute to the health disparities faced by neurodivergent populations. Therefore, the project investigates potential biases in the perception of pain when experienced by neurodivergent individuals, and explores how these biases contribute to health disparities. Previous research has identified health disparities between neurodivergent and non-neurodivergent populations, such as higher premature mortality in individuals with ADHD and autism. These differences may stem in part from differences in access to health care services, which may be influenced by implicit biases in others' pain perception. Therefore this first experiment aims to determine whether a bias exists in judgements about physical pain when the person experiencing the pain is neurodivergent. We will test whether there is a bias in the judgement of pain by neurodivergent individuals relative to non-neurodivergent individuals through the description of painful events.

title_r: Reproduction Package for FSE 2024 Submission `A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification'
abstract_r:
Reproduction Package A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification Abstract This artifact is a reproduction package for the manuscript “A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification”, submitted to FSE 2024. In the replication study, the transferability of the results reported by two prior publications on interpolation-based hardware model checking to software verification is investigated. The two publications are (1) Interpolation-Sequence-Based Model Checking (Vizel and Grumberg, 2009) and (2) Intertwined Forward-Backward Reachability Analysis Using Interpolants (Vizel, Grumberg, and Shoham, 2013). The purpose of this artifact is to reproduce the experiments conducted to validate the claims made in the above two publications. The artifact consists of source code, precompiled executables, and input data used in the evaluation of the replication study, as well as the results produced from the experiments. Specifically, it includes the source code and binaries of CPAchecker (at revision 44757 of branch “cfa-single-loop-transformation”), which implements the verification algorithms compared in the submitted manuscript, the SV-COMP ’23 benchmark suite, the experimental data generated from the evaluation, and instructions to run the tools and experiments. This reproduction package works best with the SoSy-Lab Virtual Machine, which runs Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. The VM has all the required dependencies installed. If you test this artifact with it, all installation steps below can be skipped. Contents This artifact contains the following items: README.*: this documentation fse2024-paper483.pdf: the manuscript submitted to FSE 2024 License.txt: license information of the artifact cpachecker/: a directory containing the source code and precompiled binaries of CPAchecker sv-benchmarks/: a directory containing the SV-COMP ’23 benchmark tasks used in our evaluation data-submission/: a directory containing the raw and processed data produced from our full evaluation (used in the manuscript, under paper-results/) and from a demo experiment (prepared for this reproduction package, under demo-results/) bench-defs/: a directory containing the benchmark and table definitions of the experiments (used by BenchExec, a framework for reliable benchmarking) This readme file will guide you through the following steps: Execute CPAchecker Perform experiments View the experimental results Execute CPAchecker System requirements for CPAchecker To execute CPAchecker, Java Runtime Environment (JRE) version ≥ 17 is required. For more information, please refer to cpachecker/INSTALL.md. Run verification algorithms in CPAchecker In the replication study, we compared the performance of three interpolation-based verification algorithms, namely IMC (McMillan, 2003), ISMC (Vizel and Grumberg, 2009), and DAR (Vizel, Grumberg, and Shoham, 2013). ISMC and DAR are the algorithms proposed by the two prior publications, respectively, and IMC is the first interpolation-based model-checking approach, which was used as the baseline in the two publications. All the algorithms have been implemented in CPAchecker. Below we list the commands to run the evaluated verification algorithms. These example commands use sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c as the input program. You can replace it with another program. IMC: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolation \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop imc.fallBack=false \ -setprop imc.loopBoundIncrementStrategyForBMC=CONST \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
ISMC: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolationSequence \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop imc.fallBack=false \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
DAR: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolationDualSequence \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop dar.fallBack=false \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
For more information on how to run CPAchecker, see cpachcker/README.md. Understand the output of CPAchecker The following is an example output shown on the console after an analysis is finished. 
[...redacted...] Verification result: TRUE. No property violation found by chosen configuration. More details about the verification run can be found in the directory "./output". Graphical representation included in the file "./output/Report.html".
There are 3 possible outcomes of the verification result: TRUE: the program is “safe”, i.e., it satisfies the given safety property FALSE: the program is “unsafe”, i.e., it contains a violation to the given safety property UNKNOWN: the analysis was inconclusive CPAchecker also generates an HTML report for conveniently browsing the results. Please refer to cpachecker/doc/Report.md for more information. Perform Experiments Install BenchExec We use BenchExec, a framework for reliable benchmarking and resource measurements, to perform our evaluation. Please follow the installation guide to set up the benchmarking environment. Experimental settings The settings are described in the XML file bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml. This XML file is used by BenchExec for limiting computing resources and scheduling runs. For the execution of a task, a resource limit of 2 CPU cores, 1800 seconds of CPU time, and 15 GB of memory is imposed. Run the Full Evaluation To run the full experiment over the 8813 benchmark tasks reported in the manuscript, execute the following command. 
benchexec bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml \ --tool-directory cpachecker/ -o results/ \ --read-only-dir / --overlay-dir . --hidden-dir /home/
Run Partial Evaluation The full evaluation requires roughly 6 months of CPA time on a 3.40 GHz core. To run the experiment on a subset of benchmark tasks, you could add -t <tasks_name> to the above command, where <task_name> refer to the task names defined in bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml. For example: 
benchexec bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml \ --tool-directory cpachecker/ -o results/ \ --read-only-dir / --overlay-dir . --hidden-dir /home/ \ -t ReachSafety-BitVectors
If you want to adjust the imposed resource limit, the following options can be used: 
-T <cputime_limit> -M <mem_limit>
For more information about these flags, please refer to benchexec -h. View the Experimental Results Generate Tables After the execution of an experiment, you can generate an interactive HTML by table-generator. Simply run: 
table-generator -x bench-defs/overall-slt-stats.xml \ -f html --no-diff -o results
Note that if the experiment is only performed on a single task set (via -t <tasks_name>), you have to replace bench-defs/overall-slt-stats.xml by bench-defs/subset-slt-stats.xml. Results from Our Experiments The results (both raw and processed data) of the partial run (on ReachSafety-BitVectors) and the full run obtained by our machines are in folders data-submission/demo-results/ and data-submission/paper-results/, respectively. The generated HTML tables are named overall-slt-stats.table.html under each respective folder. In the replication study, there are eight hypotheses extracted from the two prior publications. We list them below to make this document more standalone. For details, please refer to the bundled manuscript. Claims in the ISMC Publication H1.A: ISMC is faster than IMC on tasks with property violation. H1.B: ISMC is faster than IMC when IMC finds a proof only at high unrolling bounds. H1.C: Overall, ISMC is faster than IMC (by 30 % in this experiment). In our experiments, we confirmed H1.A also for software verification, but H1.B and H1.C did not hold. Claims in the DAR Publication H2.A: For DAR, the ratio between iterations using global strengthening to the total number of iterations is less than 0.5 in most tasks. H2.B: IMC finds a proof slower than DAR in many tasks even though it has a smaller convergence length. H2.C: DAR computes more interpolants than IMC. H2.D: DAR’s run-time is more sensitive to the sizes of interpolants than IMC. H2.E: Overall, DAR is faster than IMC (by 36 % in this experiment). In our experiments, we confirmed H2.A and H2.C also for software verification, but H2.B, H2.D, and H2.E did not hold. title_r: Replication and Extension Sherf and Morrison (2020)
abstract_r: Sherf and Morrison (2020) describe that employees’ self-efficacy influences the perceived value of feedback and thus how much feedback they seek. Moreover, they argue that perspective taking plays a moderating role in the relation between self-efficacy and feedback-seeking. Sherf and Morrison (2020) measured employees' valuation of feedback and observed that it mediated the relation between self-efficacy and feedback-seeking, however, that was the only benefits and costs of feedback that the authors included in their model. A common assumption in the feedback-seeking literature is that when employees consider whether to ask for feedback they conduct a mental calculation of perceived benefits and costs of such feedback (Anseel et al., 2015; Ashford, 1986; Ashford & Cummings, 1983). Extending Sherf and Morrison (2020), in this study we will examine how self-efficacy and perspective taking influence various benefits and costs of asking for feedback. Specifically, we will look at: feedback expectancy value, self-presentation and ego costs, and self-presentation and ego benefits.

title_r: Reductive Allure Effects for Psychology Phenomena – Impact of Worker Recruitment Site. A pre-registered replication of Hopkins, Weisberg, & Taylor (2016).
abstract_r: Previous research (Hopkins et al., 2016) suggests that the presentation of reductive information influences people’s ability to judge the quality of a scientific explanation. For instance, people who are presented with neuroscience jargon in an explanation of a psychological phenomenon judge those explanations more favorably than explanations without the jargon, even if that information is logically irrelevant. In a previously pre-registered (osf.io/hvm8q) attempt to replicate and extend Hopkins et al. (2016), we were unable to replicate this basic reductive explanation effect across three scientific disciplines that were included in the original study (Psychology, Neuroscience, Biology). That is, participants in our study did not rate reductive explanations significantly higher than horizontal explanations in any of these three scientific disciplines, even though we used the same testing materials and procedure as Hopkins et al. (2016). One possible explanation for our inability to replicate the reductive allure effect observed by Hopkins et al. (2016) is that we employed a different participant pool. Specifically, we recruited our participants from Prolific.co, whereas Hopkins et al. recruited participants through Amazon Mechanical Turk. Thus, in order to rule out the different participant pools as the reason for the discrepant results, we will conduct an abbreviated replication of Hopkins et al. (2016) using only their original descriptions of psychological phenomena (the scientific discipline that showed the largest reductive explanation effect) with a participant pool selected from Amazon Mechanical Turk.

title_r: Registered replication of Traczyk et al. (2018). Numerate decision makers don’t use more effortful strategies unless it pays.
abstract_r: The original study investigated skilled and adaptive strategy selection in risky decision making. We wish to replicate the effect shown by Traczyk et al. (2018), where people with higher objective statistical numeracy (measured by Berlin Numeracy Test, BNT, Cokely et al., 2012), in comparison to people with lower numeracy, adaptively select choice strategy depending on the task structure or the characteristics of the environment. Put differently, highly numerate people do not use more effortful strategies unless it is strictly required; in trivial choice problems, they employ fast and frugal heuristic processing, but in meaningful problems, they engage more elaborate and effortful information processing. We propose that people with high objective statistical numeracy are able to learn the importance of the decision problems. If it is meaningful, they are likely to deliberate longer to make a superior decision, making choices consistent with predictions of more effortful and reward maximizing choice strategies predicted by Cumulative Prospect Theory/Expected Value (CPT/EV) theory, but if the decision problems are trivial and lead to comparable payoffs, they make faster but normatively suboptimal choices consistent with predictions of fast and frugal priority heuristic (PH). Reference- Cokely, E. T., Galesic, M., Schulz, E., Garcia-Retamero, R., & Ghazal, S. (2012). Measuring Risk Literacy: The Berlin Numeracy Test. Judgment and Decision Making, 7(1), 23. Traczyk, J., Sobkow, A., Fulawka, K., Kus, J., Garcia-Retamero, R., & Petrova, D. (2018). Numerate decision makers don’t use more eﬀortful strategies unless it pays: A process tracing investigation of skilled and adaptive strategy selection in risky decision making. title_r: Replicating and Extending Experiment 1 from Garcea and Mahon (2012) using only picture stimuli
abstract_r: In daily life, when we need to have a drink, we try to find a cup. Would we find it faster according to the object's function or based on the manipulation of the object? Garcea and Mahon (2012) used a modified neuropsychological test that used the response time (RT) and accuracy as the dependent measures. Three objects were presented in a triangular arrangement at the same time in one trial. The top object was the target. One of the two lower objects had a similar function to the target object, and the other had a similar manipulation to the target object. The participants had to judge which object of a triad had a similar function to the target object or which object had a similar manipulation to the target. Results showed that manipulation judgments were slower than function judgments, regardless of whether the objects were shown as words or as pictures. This finding suggests that it is unnecessary to first retrieve knowledge of object manipulation before one can retrieve knowledge of object function (Garcea & Mahon, 2012). The results of Garcea and Mahon contrast with the outcomes of another study (Ruotolo & Kalénine, 2020). Ruotolo and Kalénine (2020) used the Visual-World-Paradigm to present four objects to the participants at the same time. One of the four objects was the target. The rest of the objects were distractors that could have a similar function as the target, or a similar manipulation, or be completely unrelated to the target. They found that distractors with similar functions or manipulations attracted more attention from participants than unrelated distractors. Moreover, the results showed that eye fixations to objects with a similar manipulation occurred faster relative to the objects with a similar function. This is in contrast with Garcea and Mahon’s study, as it suggests that similarity in manipulation leads to quicker attentional orienting than similarity in function. In the current experiment, we will replicate Experiment 1 of Garcea and Mahon (2012), using only the condition with object pictures. Aside from testing the replicability of Garcea and Mahon’s finding of faster reaction times for function than for manipulation similarity, we will also examine whether differences in real-world size might have contributed to this difference in reaction time. Specifically, we reasoned that one explanation for the finding of slower manipulation judgments than function judgments in Garcea and Mahon (2012) could be that if the target object and two lower objects in the stimulus displayed differed in their real-world size in some trials, this might have caused participants to be slower on these trials as they would need to imagine the manipulation of two objects (the target and the non-target) of different sizes in the real world to decide which one matches the target. Arguably, this would slow participants down (because it takes more time to imagine two manipulations for objects that differ in real-world size than to imagine the manipulation for two objects with similar real-world size), and it, therefore, could explain why this study found slower RTs for manipulation judgments. In replicating the experiment, we are able to make use of the exact same stimuli as Garcea and Mahon (2012), as they kindly made these available to us. According to the classification from Fisher and Sperandio (2018), 10 of the 35 objects used by Garcea and Mahon can be classified as ”big objects” and the rest of the objects can be classified as “small objects”. Among the 24 triads used for function judgments and manipulation judgments, 8 triads were comprised of objects of different sizes. Hence, we speculate that the object size may be an important factor in the previous experiment and it may affect the results. Accordingly, we hypothesize that manipulation judgments are only slower than function judgments when objects in the triad differ in real-world size.

title_r: Do LLMs Exhibit Human-Like Bayesian Judgment and Moral Inconsistency? A Replication Study of Cao et al. (2019)
abstract_r: This study replicates Cao et al. (2019) People Make the Same Bayesian Judgment They Criticize in Others using Large Language Models (LLMs) rather than human participants. Cao et al. (2019) found that humans exhibit an inconsistency in their responses - they make statistically accurate Bayesian judgments about profession likelihood based on gender, while simultaneously condemning others who make identical judgments. We examine whether contemporary LLMs (Claude Sonnet 3.7 and GPT-4o) display similar patterns of inconsistency. By comparing LLMs with different training methods and company missions, we attempt to identify whether algorithmic systems trained on human data inherit our inconsistencies or behave as more consistently Bayesian agents. This research helps our understanding of alignment in LLM systems, particularly regarding how different approaches to LLM development affect statistical reasoning versus encoded social norms.

title_r: Conceptual Replication of Mussweiler and Strack (2000, Study 2) Using Temperature Anchoring and a Season-Related LDT (2)
abstract_r: This study conceptually replicates Study 2 by Mussweiler and Strack (2000), which tested the Selective Accessibility Model (SAM) of the anchoring effect. According to SAM, anchoring occurs through the selective activation of anchor-consistent knowledge, driven by hypothesis-consistent testing and semantic priming. In the original study, participants first completed a standard comparative anchoring task (judging whether the average price of a new car was higher or lower than U.S. $11,000 or $22,000), followed by a Lexical Decision Task (LDT). After the LDT, they estimated the average price of a new car in an absolute judgment task. The results supported SAM, demonstrating a significant interaction between anchor condition and word type in the LDT. In the present study, we conducted a conceptual replication of this design, using an anchoring task involving temperature estimates and an LDT employing season-related words (summer- and winter-related words). Data collection was completed on June 10, 2025 (Japan Standard Time). As of this preregistration, the data have not yet been accessed or analyzed. This preregistration specifies the planned analysis procedures. The majority of the experimental procedures and hypotheses follow Mussweiler and Strack (2000) and our previous study (https://osf.io/hcbxu, https://osf.io/wgm94, https://osf.io/57cty).

title_r: "Explaining How Long CO2 Stays in the Atmosphere: Does It Change Attitudes Toward Climate Change?" - a replication study (Joslyn & Demnitz, 2021)
abstract_r: Aus wissenschaftlicher Perspektive ist ein kritischer Punkt der globalen Erwärmung erreicht (Ripple et al., 2017). Trotzdem scheint die Wahrnehmung von Risiken bezüglich des Klimawandels erheblich zwischen Ländern (Eurobarometer, 2014) und Individuen (Botzen et al., 2016) zu variieren. Häufig wird der Klimawandel als ein zeitlich und räumlich entferntes Problem wahrgenommen (Lorenzoni & Hulme, 2009). Insbesondere Menschen mit einer konservativen politischen Ideologie scheinen dem Klimawandel dabei kritisch gegenüberzustehen (Funk & Rainie, 2015). Um zu überprüfen, wie sich diese Einstellungen zum Klimawandel verändern lassen, untersuchten Joslyn und Demnitz (2021) anhand einer repräsentativen nationalen Stichprobe aus den USA die Auswirkungen von zwei einfachen Strategien der Klimakommunikation auf das Verständnis und die Reaktion auf den Klimawandel bei verschiedenen politischen Ideologien. Dabei kamen sie zu dem Ergebnis, dass psychologisch gezielte Klimakommunikation die Einstellung zur globalen Erwärmung unabhängig von politischer Ideologie verändern kann. Mit dem Ziel, das derzeitige Wissen über den Einfluss psychologisch gezielter Klimakommunikation auf die Einstellungen zum Klimawandel in verschiedenen Ländern und Kulturen zu erweitern, wird die Studie von Joslyn und Demnitz (2021) in der vorliegenden Studie im Kontext der deutschen Bevölkerung repliziert. Dabei wollen wir unter anderem dem in der Psychologie weit verbreiteten Phänomen Rechnung tragen, dass Replikationen viel zu selten durchgeführt und veröffentlicht werden (Neuliep & Crandall, 1993) und zum Aufbau einer kumulativen Wissensbasis beitragen (Brandt et al., 2014; Dekkers et al., 2010).

title_r: A replication and extension of Scott and Landy (2023): moral character beliefs about medical treatment options
abstract_r: Treatment adherence is a known problem in healthcare. For example, low medication use and adherence are noticed in patients with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disorder (COPD), even with a severe diagnosis (Ingebrigtsen et al., 2014). Likewise, psychiatric medication has stigma attached to it which increases the reluctance of patients to take medication. Research has shown that adolescents on psychiatric medication limited social interactions due to the shame which accompanies stigma (Kranke et al., 2010). One area to explain low treatment adherence are beliefs associated with specific treatments: for example, research has shown that the use of medication instead of behavioural or lifestyle changes is perceived to be a signal of lower willpower (Scott & Landy, 2023), while working hard and applying effort (i.e, willpower) is a socially acceptable positive moral characteristic (Amos et al., 2017). Scott and Landy's (2023) work on moral judgements about medical treatment options therefore laid the groundwork for understanding the influence of moral virtues on medical decision-making. The study revealed a bias, with a preference for behavioural or lifestyle changes over pharmaceutical interventions as it is perceived to be reflective of a stronger moral character. The current study is a partial replication and an extension of Scott and Landy's (2023) work on moral judgements about medical treatment options. The present study aims to explore this theme in the contexts of physical health (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disorder; COPD), mental health (Depression) and neurodivergent conditions (Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder). In their original study, Scott and Landy include COPD and depression, but did not compare these directly; that is, they did not examine if the effect of treatment type on moral judgements differed by type of conditions, which we expect to find given the known stigma around mental health and neurodivergence (Kranke et al., 2010). In summary, there is one main research question for this study. RQ: Does the effect of treatment type on moral judgements vary by type of conditions? References: Amos, C., Zhang, L., & Read, D. (2017). Hardworking as a heuristic for moral character: Why we attribute moral values to those who work hard and its implications. Journal of Business Ethics, 158(4), 1047–1062. Ingebrigtsen, T. E., & Landy, J. F. (2023). “good people don’t need medication”: How moral character beliefs affect medical decision making. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 175, 104225.

title_r: Reductive Allure Effects for Psychology Phenomena – Impact of Worker Recruitment Screening. A Pre-Registered Replication of Hopkins, Weisberg, & Taylor (2016).
abstract_r: Previous research (Hopkins et al., 2016) suggests that the presentation of reductive information influences people’s ability to judge the quality of a scientific explanation. For instance, people who are presented with neuroscience jargon in an explanation of a psychological phenomenon judge those explanations more favorably than explanations without the jargon, even if that information is logically irrelevant. In a previously pre-registered (osf.io/hvm8q) attempt to replicate and extend Hopkins et al. (2016), we were unable to replicate this basic reductive explanation effect across three scientific disciplines that were included in the original study (Psychology, Neuroscience, Biology). That is, participants in our study did not rate reductive explanations significantly higher than horizontal explanations in any of these three scientific disciplines, even though we used the same testing materials and procedure as Hopkins et al. (2016). One possible explanation for our inability to replicate the reductive allure effect observed by Hopkins et al. (2016) is that we employed a different participant pool. Specifically, we recruited our participants from Prolific.co, whereas Hopkins et al. recruited participants through Amazon Mechanical Turk. Thus, in order to rule out the different participant pools as the reason for the discrepant results, we conducted a second pre-registered experiment (osf.io/8af7k) to examine the effects of worker platform. In that second experiment, we conducted an abbreviated replication of Hopkins et al. (2016) using only their original descriptions of psychological phenomena (the scientific discipline that showed the largest reductive explanation effect) with a participant pool selected from Amazon Mechanical Turk. In this second experiment, we were again unable to replicate the basic reductive explanation effect for psychological phenomena found in Hopkins et al. (2016). Our failure to replicate the original reductive explanation effect in Experiment 2 was complicated by the fact that we encountered abnormally high rates of participant exclusion based on our pre-registered criteria (namely, failure on the instructions, failure on our attention check, or submission times ±3 SD away from the mean). Out of the 174 participants who completed the survey, 82 were removed, resulting in an exclusion rate greater than 40%. This excessively high exclusion rate raises serious concern about the quality of our data, even for the participants who were not excluded. As such, our inability to replicate Hopkins et al. (2016) may have resulted from a generally inattentive participant pool. To address this concern, we will attempt a third replication of Hopkins et al. (2016). In this third replication, we will use the same procedure as described in Experiment 2 (osf.io/8af7k), however, we will recruit MTURK participants using CloudResearch, a third-party website that pre-screens MTURK workers to improved data quality. In this way, we will limit our recruitment to “approved” workers that are more likely to produce high-quality data with an acceptable exclusion rate.

title_r: Exact replication of Kozłowska et al. (2023) The Napoleon complex, revisited: Those high on the Dark Triad traits are dissatisfied with their height and are short
abstract_r: The dark triad is a personality taxonomy that, unlike the Big Five, focuses primarily on negative social personality traits: Psychopathy, Narcissism, and Machiavellianism. It has attracted much attention over the past 20 years after Paulhurst et al. coined the term in 2002, and research on the correlation between Dark Triad traits and other factors has increased drastically. One such example is the correlation of the Dark Triad traits with height dissatisfaction and with physical height itself. Kozłowska et al. recently published these results (2023) and concluded that the theory of the so-called "Napoleon complex" seems to be correct. Briefly summarized, the "Napoleon complex" is the idea that smaller men are at a disadvantage and compensate for this through negative behavior. In their results, Kozłowska et al. found that there was a significant negative correlation between Dark Triad traits and height in men. They also found that those scoring high on Dark Triad traits are more dissatisfied with their own height. This is interesting because it is one of the first studies to examine the relationship between Dark Triad traits and attitudes towards height, as well as physical height. Other studies of height in psychology often show no, or a positive, correlation. Therefore, it is of interest to conduct an exact replication study to verify or reject these findings in order to strengthen the current evidence base and thus lay the groundwork for further research on this topic.

title_r: Acquiring false information from narrative fictions: A conceptual replication and extension of Appel & Richter (2007)
abstract_r: Within the planned study, narrative fictions are understood as written stories that primarily deal with non-real events, objects and persons, whereby this limited reference to reality is both intended by the author and recognized by the recipients (e.g., Gertken & Köppe, 2009). Although people often encounter narrative fictions in everyday life, relatively little empirical research has been conducted on their psychological effects and the underlying mechanisms. Existing studies show that factually incorrect information embedded in narrative fictions can cause substantial changes in readers' beliefs despite the known limited reference to reality (e.g., Rapp et al., 2014). In one of the few studies on the topic that includes more than one measurement point, Appel and Richter (2007) demonstrated that such changes in belief can even increase over time – a phenomenon that corresponds to an absolute sleeper effect. Here, 81 participants recruited through a university (mostly students) read either a fictional story that contained both true and false claims about real-world issues, or a control story. There were great short-term persuasion effects from the false information; these effects were even greater in a group with a 2-week measurement delay. Belief certainty (i.e., how sure the readers were of their beliefs) was reduced immediately after reading, but returned to the baseline level after 2 weeks. The pattern of findings was interpreted in such a way that beliefs acquired through reading fictional narratives are integrated into world knowledge. The aim of the planned experiment is a conceptual replication and extension of this study. The experiment is planned to be identical to the original study except for two major differences: first, the participants will not be recruited at a university only in order that the generalizability of findings extends to a broader population; secondly, different reading stimuli (based on an excerpt from Homer's Odyssey) will be used than in Appel and Richter (2007). This will help clarify whether the findings occur independently of this specific textual material.

title_r: Prevalence-induced Concept Change in the Judgement of Male Bodies: A Replication and Extension of Devine et al. (2023)
abstract_r: The following study aims to replicate H1b from Devine et al. (2023). Here, the authors found that men were sensitive to prevalence-induced concept changes (PICC) when judging whether male bodies varying in muscularity were muscular or not, but not when judging whether male bodies varying in body fat were overweight or not. Furthermore, they found that men were overall faster in judging whether a body is muscular compared to judging whether a body is overweight. Taken together, these results lead the authors to suspect that men might have an attentional bias towards idealized male bodies, which manifests in faster and more selective extraction of muscle-related body information. Thus, Devine et al. show that PICC may not represent a general perceptual effect, but rather could be moderated by the specific stimulus category. Our main goal of the current study is to replicate the effect found that the strength of PICC in the judgment of male bodies depends on the specific stimulus category (weight-related, muscle-related). Furthermore, we intend to replicate the difference in response times between the judgments of these stimulus categories. The study design will be adjusted to control for possible confounding factors such as the order of the presented stimulus category. In addition, the stimulus material (computer-generated male bodies) will be adapted in order to achieve better comparability between the stimulus categories. Furthermore, we will examine whether the degree of body dissatisfaction (BD) related to different body characteristics (weight-related, muscle-related) influences whether participants judge muscle-related bodies faster than weight-related bodies, or vice versa. Recent studies suggest that attentional biases toward body-related stimuli specifically affect men with higher BD rather than the general population, and that the impact might differ depending on whether men experience more muscle-related or weight-related BD (Joseph et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2018; Porras-Garcia et al., 2020; Talbot & Saleme, 2022; Kirby et al., 2023). Therefore, BD will be measured separately for both stimulus categories (weight-related, muscle-related) (Ralph-Nearman & Filik, 2018).

title_r: Registered Replication Report : Strack, Martin, & Stepper (1988)
abstract_r: According to the facial feedback hypothesis, people’s affective responses can be influenced by their own facial expression (e.g., smiling, pouting), even when their expression did not result from their emotional experiences. For example, Strack, Martin, and Stepper (1988) instructed participants to rate the funniness of cartoons using a pen that they held in their mouth. In line with the facial feedback hypothesis, when participants held the pen with their teeth (inducing a “smile”), they rated the cartoons as funnier than when they held the pen with their lips (inducing a “pout”). This seminal study of the facial feedback hypothesis has not been replicated directly. This Registered Replication Report describes the results of 17 independent direct replications of Study 1 from Strack et al. (1988), all of which followed the same vetted protocol. A meta-analysis of these studies examined the difference in funniness ratings between the “smile” and “pout” conditions. The original Strack et al. (1988) study reported a rating difference of 0.82 units on a 10-point Likert scale. Our meta-analysis revealed a rating difference of 0.03 units with a 95% confidence interval ranging from −0.11 to 0.16.

title_r: Do infants prefer prosocial others? A direct replication of Hamlin & Wynn (2011)
abstract_r: Within the last five years, social sciences, especially psychology, have seen problems with replicability and reproducibility. A growing body of evidence suggests that low powered studies, undisclosed statistical flexibility and lack of pre-specified study standards are all contributing factors to a low rate of replicability. Within the realm of infant social evaluation, a topic of both theoretical interest and empirical controversy, both replications and non- replications exist. Given this, and the movement toward replication in psychology in general, this paper will present results both a pre-registered sample and a larger sample that directly replicates Hamlin & Wynn’s (2011) “box scenario”, which examines whether preverbal infants prefer prosocial to antisocial others. Our pre-registered sample did not replicate the original finding seen in Hamlin & Wynn (2011). However, when including all infants tested in the box scenario, the finding did indeed replicate. Overall, our findings add to the scientific understanding of infant social evaluation and provide an important opportunity to add to the replicability movement.

title_r: Replication and extension of: Large language models associate Muslims with violence by Abid et al., 2021
abstract_r: The main purpose of this study is to replicate and extend the results in Abid et al. (2021; Nature Machine Intelligence). Building on preliminary evidence provided by the creators of GPT-2 and GPT-3 (state-of-the-art text generation algorithms; Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020), the authors showed biased automated text generation when religious identities are cued in text completion prompts. GPT-3 completions for prompts formatted as “Two X walk into a” contained violent content much more often if X was replaced with “Muslims” rather than adjectives signifying other major religions. Since the smallest difference was found between “Muslim” and “Christian”, our replication attempt focuses on this more conservative measure of the model’s religion bias. However, we include the “Hindu” category as well to control for the impact of majority/minority difference between “Muslim” and “Christian”. We extend these results by exploring whether naming specific individuals changes the propensity of the model to rely on biased group-level representations. For instance, using “Y walks into a” or "Y and Z walk into a" where Y and Z are replaced with common Muslim names compared with names common among adherents of Christianity and Hinduism. We also examine whether the model is sensitive to differing degrees of genericity in the main referent of prompts, which can vary along a continuum. Generic kinds like “Muslim” lie near one end of the spectrum. Individual celebrities whose personal information presumably features strongly in GPT-3’s training data (from CommonCrawl.org), lie near the other end. Common names associated with social kinds like “Muslim” (e.g., Ali Islam) are somewhere in-between, albeit closer to the specific end of the genericity spectrum. Before the first experiment was performed, we expected reduced bias as the specificity of the prompts are increased. Please note that the supplementary materials linked below on PsyArxiv are not anonymized. Anonymized versions of the study's earlier, more detailed ArXiv preprint as well as the supplementary materials can be found within this repository instead. ChatGPT data can be found in the Data folder, but is not discussed in these earlier manuscripts.

title_r: Replication Study of Baron (2022): School Spending and Student Outcomes
abstract_r: Baron (2022) explores the independent effects of operational expenditure and capital expenditure on student outcomes in school districts across Wisconsin from the outcomes of close referendum approvals. By utilizing a dynamic regression discontinuity framework and cubic specification, the author finds that narrowly passing an operational referendum, increases operational expenditure per pupil by $298 each year on average, following the referendum over a ten year period. From this $198 are spent on instructional expenses. These point estimates are statistically significant at the 10% and 5% level, respectively. We first reproduce the main results from the paper without any issues arising. Secondly, we conduct a robustness replicability to (1) dropping school districts from the top and bottom 5% of the revenue limits distribution, categorically, and (2) dividing the time frame of the study into two periods: 1996-2005 and 2005-2014. We find that dropping the top 5% of the school districts by revenue limits reduces the additional operational expenditure by $140 per pupil (lower by 50 percent) and the effects of passing an operational referendum were nearly double in the former period compared to the latter period. Lastly, we find that the estimated effects on student outcomes rely heavily on recent observations.

title_r: Do People Really Think They Are Alone In A Crowd Of Sheep?: Replication And Extension Of Pronin Et Al. (2007)
abstract_r: People often think they are less biased, more rational, and less likely to conform than their peers. For example, research by Pronin, Berger, and Molouki (2007) found that Princeton students evaluated themselves as much less likely to conform compared to the average Princeton student. Although the results were convincing, this study was conducted using only 40 participants from a prestigious university, which raises potential concerns about the replicability and generalizability of their findings. We replicated this study in order to generalize the findings to a broader range of participants and use a larger sample size. We also extended the previous research to assess if participants would evaluate a close friend the same as the self in regard to perceptions of conformity. Consistent with the original study, we found that ASU students thought they conformed less than their peers. However, they reported that their close friend conformed as much as their peers. The results of our replication generalize the original findings to a new sample of participants and also show that this effect is specific to perceptions of the self vs. others and not when comparing a close friend to others.

title_r: Modeling Help Seeking Intentions In Victims Of Intimate Partner Violence: A Conceptual Replication Of Fleming And Resick (2017)
abstract_r: Victims of intimate partner violence come forward and seek services and help for the crimes committed upon them at much lower rates than victims of other interpersonal crimes. In this study, the Theory of Planned Behavior was used to assess individual behavioral predictors of formal help-seeking in victims of intimate partner violence in order to better understand factors that promote or inhibit help-seeking in this vulnerable population, including victims’ attitudes about help seeking, the subjective norms they feel about help seeking, their perceived ability to get help, and the relationship these factors have with prior experiences. Partial support was found for the full Theory of Planned Behavior model predicting intentions for all resource types, with attitudes and perceived behavioral control predicting intentions for most resources, while norms rarely contributed to the variance. Prior experience was related to attitudes about several of the resources.

title_r: Replication Study of Cook et al (2023): The Evolution of Access to Public Accomodations in the United States
abstract_r: This is a replication study of Cook et al.(2023), a paper that investigates the determinants of access to nondiscriminatory public accommodations for African-Americans before the 1964 Civil Rights Act. They utilize the Negro Motorist Green Books and World War II casualty data to examine the impact of demographic shifts caused by wartime casualties on the prevalence of nondiscriminatory establishments. Using a difference-in-differences approach, they show that a 10% increase in white casualties led to a 0.6% increase in nondiscriminatory businesses. Further, an instrumental variable strategy indicates that a 10% rise in the Black population share correlated with increased nondiscriminatory services. Our replication study shows that the difference-in-differences estimates remain stable even after excluding states with the highest average white World War II casualties or Southern states. However, the instrumental variable estimates become sensitive to the use of robust standard errors. The reproduction of the figures and tables of the paper is mostly accurate, with a minor discrepancy in Table 3 Panel A column 3, where the original coefficient is stated as 0.0191, and the replicated coefficient is found to be 0.0263.

title_r: Registered Replication Report: Strack, Martin, & Stepper, 1988
abstract_r: According to the facial feedback hypothesis, people’s affective responses can be influenced by their own facial expression (e.g., smiling, pouting), even when their expression did not result from their emotional experiences. For example, Strack, Martin, and Stepper (1988) instructed participants to rate the funniness of cartoons using a pen that they held in their mouth. In line with the facial feedback hypothesis, when participants held the pen with their teeth (inducing a “smile”), they rated the cartoons as funnier than when they held the pen with their lips (inducing a “pout”). This seminal study of the facial feedback hypothesis has not been replicated directly. This Registered Replication Report describes the results of 17 independent direct replications of Study 1 from Strack et al. (1988), all of which followed the same vetted protocol. A meta-analysis of these studies examined the difference in funniness ratings between the “smile” and “pout” conditions. The original Strack et al. (1988) study reported a rating difference of 0.82 units on a 10-point Likert scale. Our meta-analysis revealed a rating difference of 0.03 units with a 95% confidence interval ranging from −0.11 to 0.16. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)

title_r: Successful Replication of "The Long-Run Effects of Sports Club Vouchers for Primary School Children (2022)"
abstract_r: Marcus, Siedler and Ziebarth (2022 American Economic Journal: Economic Policy) examine the long-run health effects of a universal sports-club voucher program that was introduced in Saxony for primary school children in 2009. In 2018, the authors designed a survey that targeted the affected cohorts and nearby cohorts in Saxony and two neighboring states, and use a differences-in-differences identification strategy that exploits variation across states and cohorts in policy exposure. The authors document that treated individuals have knowledge of the program and recall receiving and redeeming the vouchers at higher rates, but find no effects on any health outcomes or behaviors. We successfully reproduce the main results of the paper exactly using data available in the paper's replication package and new Stata and R code. We also verify the robustness of the results using different outcomes, different control variables, different sample restrictions and different inference methods.

title_r: Reply to Nicholas et al. Using a ResNet-18 network to detect features of Alzheimer’s disease on functional magnetic resonance imaging: a failed replication. Comment on “Odusami et al. Analysis of features of Alzheimer’s disease: detection of early stage from functional brain changes in magnetic resonance images using a finetuned ResNet18 Network. Diagnostics 2021, 11, 1071” /
abstract_r: We have studied the manuscript of Nicholas et al. [1] very attentively; here are our comments: The authors have used a different dataset (ADNI-3, rather than ADNI-2 used in [2]). The protocols of ADNI-2 and ADNI-3 datasets are not fully consistent [3]. The ADNI MR data set includes a wide range of scanner platforms; however, there has been a broad gap between older MRI systems and the state-of-the-art systems within each vendor’s product line. In ADNI-3, the “ADNI 3 Basic” and “ADNI 3 Advanced” protocols were used. The authors failed to mention if the images they used were made using a protocol compatible with ADNI-2. The dMRI spatial resolution was improved between ADNI-2 and ADNI-3 by reducing the voxel size from 2.7 x 2.7 x 2.7 mm to 2.0 x 2.0 x 2.0 mm [4]. This may have influenced the results. Moreover, the classification results among these studies are not directly comparable, because they differ in terms of the sets of participants. We fully agree that the replication of important findings by multiple independent investigators is fundamental to the accumulation of scientific evidence [5]. Deep learning network models are notoriously known for being difficult to replicate, even if the same sets of parameters are used. The training of neural network models is not deterministic, so the models are likely to produce differing results [6]. The strive of the authors to precisely replicate the results may not be achievable. [...].

title_r: Public Infrastructure and Economic Development: Evidence from Postal Systems A Replication Study of Rogowski et al. (American Journal of Political Science, 2022)
abstract_r: Rogowski et al. (2022) use secondary data to study the impact of historic postal infrastructure on economic development, both cross-country and within the US. Their results suggest a large positive effect of post offices on economic development that is robust across various sensitivity checks. We successfully computationally reproduce all results. In a robustness assessment, we find the results to be robust to simple changes in the analysis but observe some sensitivity to accounting for spatial trends in the long-term cross-country analysis. Despite this, we find the results to be overall robust given the numerous analyses and robustness checks in the original paper.

title_r: Do Reading Goals Make a Difference for Refutation Text Effectiveness? A conceptual replication of Asberger et al. (2024 )
abstract_r: There are many misconceptions about educational topics. For instance, it is a widespread assumption that differences in hemispheric dominance (left brain, right brain), originally and scientifically referring to task-related specialization in the brain, can explain individual differences between learners. To overcome such misconceptions, refutation texts appear to be a promising approach. However, it is yet an open question, which factors influence the effectiveness of refutation texts. One factor that possibly influences the effectiveness of refutation interventions may be individuals’ reading goals. A recent study (Asberger et al., 2024, https://doi.org/10.1080/00220973.2024.2358480) showed mixed results regarding the influence of reading goals on conceptual change. We will follow up on their study to further investigate whether different reading goals (reading for an explanation vs. for entertainment) moderate potential effects of a refutation text to elicit conceptual change within preservice teachers about an educational neuromyth (i.e. hemispheric dominance). Specifically, we study in which way text type (refutation vs. traditional text), reading goal (for an explanation vs. for entertainment) and time (before vs. after reading the respective text type) interact and affect beliefs in the hemispheric dominance neuromyth and their confidence-accuracy. The primary change compared to Asberger et al. (2024) concerns the operationalization of the reading goal instructions.

title_r: Felt and Perceived Musical Emotions: A Replication and Extension of Kallinen and Ravaja (2006)
abstract_r: In music and emotion research, a crucial consideration is the relationship between felt and perceived emotions. A key study in understanding these relationships was published by Kallinen and Ravaja (2006) titled “Emotion perceived and emotion felt: Same and different”, in which five empirical hypotheses were investigated. However, this study has never been replicated. This study aimed to replicate and conceptually extend Kallinen and Ravaja (2006). Participants (N = 60, mean age = 31.93) listened to 12 one-minute music excerpts selected a priori to express one of four basic emotions (joy, sadness, anger, fear), and provide ratings for 16 emotion adjectives (to calculate dimensions of valence, arousal, positive activation, and negative activation), first for emotions perceived in the music, and second for emotions felt by the participant. Participants completed trait inventories including behavioural inhibition and activation scales, neurotic-anxiety and sensation-seeking questionnaires, and trait empathy measures. Our replication largely reproduced results from the 2006 study: Felt valence was overall more positive than perceived, with opposite patterns found for arousal, positive activation and negative activation; emotion ratings also varied across music expressing joy, sadness, and fear. However, no effects of individual trait characteristics were replicated. Although successful, this replication differs from the original research in its interpretation of how data support the empirical hypotheses, suggesting little support for any hypothesis. Findings highlight complexities of replicating psychological research, and the importance of hypothesis-driven research to develop from theoretical models that enable specific predictions and outline the conditions for relevant evidence.

title_r: When less confident forecasts signal more expertise: A close replication of Study 1 (Palmeira & Heath, 2025)
abstract_r: This project is a close replication of Study 1 from the paper 'When less confident forecasts signal more expertise' by Palmeira and Heath (2025). The primary objective is to verify the finding that cognitive reflection moderates the relationship between an advisor's expressed confidence and their perceived expertise. Specifically, we aim to replicate the reversal of the confidence heuristic, where individuals with higher cognitive reflection scores (CRT) prefer moderately confident advisors over highly confident ones, whereas individuals with lower CRT scores show the opposite preference. We will use the original materials (economist scenario) and the modified CRT scale described in the original study. All study materials will be translated into Czech for data collection which will be done on a sample from the Czech population.

title_r: Exact replication of Kozłowska et al. (2023) The Napoleon complex, revisited: Those high on the Dark Triad traits are dissatisfied with their height and are short
abstract_r: The dark triad is a personality taxonomy that, unlike the Big Five, focuses primarily on negative social personality traits: Psychopathy, Narcissism, and Machiavellianism. It has attracted much attention over the past 20 years after Paulhurst et al. coined the term in 2002, and research on the correlation between Dark Triad traits and other factors has increased drastically. One such example is the correlation of the Dark Triad traits with height dissatisfaction and with physical height itself. Kozłowska et al. recently published these results (2023) and concluded that the theory of the so-called "Napoleon complex" seems to be correct. Briefly summarized, the "Napoleon complex" is the idea that smaller men are at a disadvantage and compensate for this through negative behavior. In their results, Kozłowska et al. found that there was a significant negative correlation between Dark Triad traits and height in men. They also found that those scoring high on Dark Triad traits are more dissatisfied with their own height. This is interesting because it is one of the first studies to examine the relationship between Dark Triad traits and attitudes towards height, as well as physical height. Other studies of height in psychology often show no, or a positive, correlation. Therefore, it is of interest to conduct an exact replication study to verify or reject these findings in order to strengthen the current evidence base and thus lay the groundwork for further research on this topic. This study is an exact replication study of a cross-sectional study. By using an online questionnaire and replicating the statistical analysis, we hope to answer the research questions of the original study: 1. are characteristics of the dark triad associated with the desire to be taller, 2. are characteristics of the dark triad associated with shorter height, and 3. are the correlations stronger in men than in women. For this purpose, we will recruit 616 participants through the study platform 'Prolific' to answer the following questionnaires and baseline information anonymously: 1. Dark Triad Dirty Dozen Questionnaire. 2. Height Dissatisfaction Subscale of the Male Body Attitudes Scale. 3. Demographic data. We will analyze the hypotheses using the same statistical methods as in the original study, i.e., Pearson correlation coefficient, Fischer Z-transformation, Steiger's Z-test, and multiple linear regressions.

title_r: Felt and Perceived Musical Emotions: A Replication and Extension of Kallinen and Ravaja (2006)
abstract_r: In music and emotion research, a crucial consideration is the relationship between felt and perceived emotions. A key study in understanding these relationships was published by Kallinen and Ravaja (2006) titled “Emotion perceived and emotion felt: Same and different”, in which five empirical hypotheses were investigated. However, this study has never been replicated. This study aimed to replicate and conceptually extend Kallinen and Ravaja (2006). Participants (N = 60, mean age = 31.93) listened to 12 one-minute music excerpts selected a priori to express one of four basic emotions (joy, sadness, anger, fear), and provide ratings for 16 emotion adjectives (to calculate dimensions of valence, arousal, positive activation, and negative activation), first for emotions perceived in the music, and second for emotions felt by the participant. Participants completed trait inventories including behavioural inhibition and activation scales, neurotic-anxiety and sensation-seeking questionnaires, and trait empathy measures. Our replication largely reproduced results from the 2006 study: Felt valence was overall more positive than perceived, with opposite patterns found for arousal, positive activation and negative activation; emotion ratings also varied across music expressing joy, sadness, and fear. However, no effects of individual trait characteristics were replicated. Although successful, this replication differs from the original research in its interpretation of how data support the empirical hypotheses, suggesting little support for any hypothesis. Findings highlight complexities of replicating psychological research, and the importance of hypothesis-driven research to develop from theoretical models that enable specific predictions and outline the conditions for relevant evidence.

title_r: Registered Replication Report: Rand, Greene & Nowak(2012)
abstract_r: In an anonymous 4-person economic game, participants contributed more money to a common project (i.e., cooperated) when required to decide quickly than when forced to delay their decision (Rand, Greene & Nowak, 2012), a pattern consistent with the “social heuristics” hypothesis proposed by Rand and colleagues. The results of studies using time pressure have been mixed, with some replication attempts observing similar patterns (e.g., Rand et al., 2014) and others observing null effects (e.g., Tinghög et al., 2013, Verkoeijen et al., 2014). This Registered Replication Report (RRR) assessed the size and variability of the effect of time pressure on cooperative decisions by combining 21 separate, pre-registered replications of the critical conditions from Study 7 of the original paper (Rand et al., 2012). The primary planned analysis used data from all participants who were randomly assigned to conditions and who met the protocol inclusion criteria (an intent-to-treat approach that included the 65.9% of participants in the Time Pressure condition and 7.5% in the Forced Delay condition who did not adhere to the time constraints), and observed a difference in contributions of -0.37 percentage points, compared to an 8.6 percentage point difference calculated from the original data. Analyzing the data as the original paper did, including data only for participants who complied with the time constraints, the RRR observed a 10.37 percentage point difference in contributions compared to a 15.31 percentage point difference in the original study. In combination, the results of the intent-to-treat analysis and the compliant-only analysis are consistent with the presence of selection biases and the absence of a causal effect of time pressure on cooperation

title_r: Migration, Diversity, and Economic Growth. A Replication Study of Bove and Elia (World Development, 2017)
abstract_r: This study examines the antecedents of Mobile banking (M-banking) app adoption, explores post-adoption effects, and tests the moderating effect of consumer status orientation on the relationship between adoption intention and its consequences. The conceptual model hypothesized 20 relationships, including 10 moderations. Hypotheses are tested using the structural equation modeling method (PLS-SEM) on a sample of 509 individuals. The results reveal that the main variables of 'users' rational perception, namely behavioral control and terminal security, significantly influence the intention to adopt the application, which in turn impact relationship quality and financial inclusion. However, hedonic expectations do not have a significant impact on the intention to adopt the application; the impact of culture in these relationships is further established; indeed, traditional and modern values moderate the impact of the intention to adopt the application on key post-adoption factors, financial inclusion, and relationship quality. The main recommendations and limitations of the research are discussed.A recent and well known paper, Bove and Elia (2017), argues that migrants' diversity, as captured by the indexes of both fractionalization and polarization, exerts a positive effect on GDP growth. In fact, by using the same dataset and methodology, we show that the impact of diversity cannot be distinguished from that of migration itself due to the very high correlation among the corresponding variables. Also, if one disentangles migration from diversity, following Alesina et al. (2016), only migration maintains a positive impact on growth while diversity, as captured by fractionalization, turns out to be weakly and positively associated with growth, but limitedly to the 1980-2010 time span. Polarization, on the other hand, does not seem to exert any effect on growth. The question as to whether diversity is more or less beneficial in terms of economic growth remains therefore an intriguing one, and calls for more theoretical and empirical analyses, possibly based on less (geographically) aggregated data.

title_r: Do LLMs Exhibit Human-Like Bayesian Judgment and Moral Inconsistency? A Replication Study of Cao et al. (2019)
abstract_r: This study replicates Cao et al. (2019) People Make the Same Bayesian Judgment They Criticize in Others using Large Language Models (LLMs) rather than human participants. Cao et al. (2019) found that humans exhibit an inconsistency in their responses - they make statistically accurate Bayesian judgments about profession likelihood based on gender, while simultaneously condemning others who make identical judgments. We examine whether contemporary LLMs (Claude Sonnet 3.7 and GPT-4o) display similar patterns of inconsistency. By comparing LLMs with different training methods and company missions, we attempt to identify whether algorithmic systems trained on human data inherit our inconsistencies or behave as more consistently Bayesian agents. This research helps our understanding of alignment in LLM systems, particularly regarding how different approaches to LLM development affect statistical reasoning versus encoded social norms.

title_r: Exploring Links Between Aural Lexical Knowledge and L2 Listening in Arabic and Japanese Speakers: A Close Replication of Cheng, Matthews, Lange and McLean (2022)
abstract_r: Aural lexical knowledge (ALK) is crucial for second language (L2) listening. Despite its importance, there is scant research that has validly explored the relationship between ALK and L2 listening across different English as a Foreign Language (EFL) contexts. In an effort to broaden this research base, the current study closely replicates a previous study, Cheng et al. (2022), which measured single-word ALK, phrasal verb ALK and L2 listening comprehension among participants with Chinese as a first language (L1). The current study administered the same instruments but did so among 147 Japanese and 131 Arabic-speaking English language learners. Results indicated that the capacity of ALK to predict variance in L2 listening for the Japanese group (R2 = .38) was similar to that observed in the original study (R2 = .42). However, the results for the Arabic-speaking group were very different to that of the original study and showed an unexpectedly strong relationship between ALK and L2 listening (R2 = .92). Future research directions and pedagogical implications are discussed.

title_r: Assessing inconsistent responding in digital and paper formats: a replication study using the TIMSS 2023 Confidence in Mathematics scale in Ireland
abstract_r: This study replicates and extends previous research on inconsistent responding in mixed-worded scales. Using a posttest-only experimental design, we examine the prevalence of inconsistent responding on the TIMSS 2023 Confidence in Mathematics Scale by comparing randomly equivalent digital and paper questionnaire administrations in Ireland. Two detection methods are employed: Mean Absolute Difference and Factor Mixture Analysis. Results indicate slightly higher rates of inconsistent responding in digital than in paper administration formats across most comparisons. Also, fourth-grade students exhibited higher rates of inconsistent responding compared to eighth-grade students. The study further investigates the role of student characteristics in predicting inconsistent responding. Among student background and digital-specific variables considered in binary logistic regression models, mathematics achievement was the only systematic negative predictor of inconsistent responding, explaining most of the variance, especially in younger students. This study highlights the importance of considering administration mode in large-scale assessments and provides implications for survey methodology, especially as digital testing becomes more widespread.

title_r: Replication and extension of Pitcher's 2011 JNeuro article: "Two Critical and Functionally Distinct Stages of Face Perception"
abstract_r: Here we like to re-investigate the exp1 of the TMS-face perception study, where the TMS on the right OFA (compared to sham sites, like vertex) on both the 40-50 ms and the 110-120 ms time periods (among 30-40, 50-60, 70-80, 90-100, 110-120,130-140, and 150-160 ms ranges, 7 options) and comparing the face intact vs. face feature (i.e., eye change) delayed-matching task, subjects' (N=16) performance were significantly worse. We like to both replicate these famous phenomenon, while also adding another condition called 'eye distance changes', known to be a 2nd-order configural cues that might be better mediated by FFA (but not OFA). Since TMS the OFA should only affect the 'eye change' (the first level) face discrimination, we expect that the TMS effect will be replicated in TMS-OFA and on the eye-change condition, especially during the 110-120 ms period, whereas the TMS to the OFA might have an interference in the eye-distance change in the putative 150-160 ms period, since that's when the influence to the FFA (via OFA) will be more robust. Another difference from the original research is that our prime stimulus presentation time will be determined by the average of the stimulus durations of the last four reversal points of one or two 50-trial staircase sessions. The purpose of this staircase addition is to ensure that every participant performs in the 80% accuracy, whose 1st stimulus presentation time may be variable across participants.

title_r: Balanced vs. Skewed Input in L2 Argument Construction Learning: A Replication and Extension of Casenhiser and Goldberg (2005)
abstract_r: The paper compares the effectiveness of balanced and skewed input at facilitating the acquisition of a novel construction by learners of English as a foreign language. The study replicates and extends Casenhiser and Godberg’s (2005) seminal paper on L1 construction acquisition. The study argues that the previous research did not pay sufficient attention to the frequency-prototypicality connection, as observed in natural language usage, and makes an attempt to overcome this limitation by adopting a more principled approach to this issue, which takes into consideration the frequency effects. Polish university students (N = 80) were randomly assigned either to skewed frequency groups, where the input was skewed towards the prototypical exemplars of the novel appearance construction, or a balanced frequency group, where the input was evenly distributed among the exemplars of this construction. Both groups were tested on comprehension of the target structure. The results suggest a facilitative effect of balanced input, as compared to the skewed input. This result was found to be correlated with the degree of cognitive/experiential entrenchment of the situations coded by the test exemplars, that is, the balanced frequency group significantly outperformed the control group only on tasks depicting highly familiar and frequently encountered scenes.

title_r: Task-induced involvement, motivation and second language vocabulary learners: replicating and extending Hulstijn & Laufer (2001)
abstract_r: This study is a replication and extension of Hulstijn and Laufer (2001) and focuses on English learners' incidental learning of vocabulary in specific task conditions and factors that affect this learning. Using Laufer and Hulstijn's (2001) Involvement Load Hypothesis (ILH) as a basis for examining task effectiveness, we explore EFL learners' vocabulary learning in three task conditions: Reading, Reading Plus Fill-In, and Writing. Beyond the task effects, the study extends the original design by examining learners' gains at different levels of lexical mastery, measuring their motivation and task engagement, and including interview-based qualitative findings exploring their experiences and perceptions of participation. Findings indicate that Reading was the least effective condition in terms of vocabulary learning, with Reading Plus and Writing resulting in similar lexical gains, only partially confirming Hulstijn and Laufer (2001). As regards task engagement, there were no statistical differences in participants self-reported scores across groups, but the dynamic nature of their engagement was evident, as was the role of their emotions. Based on these findings, we present a theoretical and methodological discussion of the ILH in terms of its use, interpretation and predictions of task effects on vocabulary learning. We also underline the value of replication research and call for more cross-disciplinary research approaches in this area, particularly in relation to learner-related variables.

title_r: Shape effects on consumer choice: A conceptual replication of Wang et al. (2017) "Assessing the effect of shape on the evaluation of expected and actual chocolate flavour"
abstract_r: This project contains materials and data from a conceptual replication of Wang et al. (2017; DOI: 10.1186/s13411-017-0052-1) examining whether cookie shape influences consumer choice. Hypothesis: Round shapes (circle, heart) are chosen more frequently than angular shapes (square, triangle, star) in pairwise comparisons. Method: Within-subjects experiment (N = 6 pilot), 10 paired comparisons, stimuli identical except shape. Implemented in PsychoPy 2023.2.3. Main result: Binomial logistic regression with random effects revealed round shapes were chosen with OR = 4.11 (β = 1.41, SE = 0.58, z = 2.43, p = 0.02). Partial support for H₁. Repository contents: stimuli (cookie images), experiment file (.psyexp + conditions.csv), raw data, JASP analysis outputs, full study documentation.

title_r: A Close Replication of Rogers et al. (2017), Study 1: Truth, Paltering, and Lying in an Incentivized Used-Car Negotiation
abstract_r: This project is a replication of Study 1 from Rogers, T., Zeckhauser, R., Gino, F., Norton, M. I., & Schweitzer, M. E. (2017). Artful paltering: The risks and rewards of using truthful statements to mislead others. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 112(3), 456–473. https://doi.org/10.1037/pspi0000081 The original study examined whether people are more willing to use paltering — a truthful but misleading statement — than to tell an explicit lie by commission in an incentivized negotiation. Participants imagine they are trying to sell a used car. A potential buyer asks whether the car has ever had problems. Participants are told two facts are true: the car failed to start twice in the past year and required repairs, and the car also drives smoothly and recently started in very cold weather. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions. In the paltering condition, they choose between disclosing the car's starting problems and sending a truthful but selectively positive response. In the lying condition, they choose between disclosing the starting problems and falsely stating that the car has never had problems. Participants are told their choice affects their probability of selling the car and earning a $1 bonus: the honest-disclosure option gives a 30% chance; the paltering response gives a 60% chance; the lie gives an 80% chance. We examine whether participants are more likely to choose the misleading response in the paltering condition than in the lying condition, even though the lie offers a higher probability of earning the bonus, and how participants evaluate the misleading response in terms of deceptiveness, honesty, and ethicality.
